Amiel Melburn Trust Archive

The Amiel Melburn Trust Archive (banmarchive.org.uk) is, in its About page's words, "an indexed and searchable online database of socialist and radical writings", and on its home page "an online database of socialist and radical writings" (banmarchive.org.uk), the kind under which the maryleelabor census record enters it and asks of it the census's question: "Whose record does it keep, who holds it, and does it keep the losing side in a form that could be taken up later?" (maryleelabor record). Its own page titles read "Amiel Melburn Trust Archive - Amiel Melburne Trust Archive" (banmarchive.org.uk), and the record gives Amiel Melburn Archive, Amiel Melburne Trust Archive and banmarchive as its other names, places it in two of the census's six areas, movement documents and archives and custody, and gives periodical runs and movement documents as its kinds of evidence (maryleelabor record).

It is the Barry Amiel and Norman Melburn Trust's: its pages carry "© Barry Amiel and Norman Melburn Trust" and "Registered Charity No. 281239", link to the Trust's website and its lectures, and call the Trust "a non-profit charitable organisation" (banmarchive.org.uk), and the Trust's site lists it as its "Online library", the "Amiel & Melburn Trust Internet Archive" (amielandmelburn.org.uk). The record names the operator as the Trust, "Registered Charity No. 281239, London; site by Common Knowledge", and the holder as "a registered charity" whose "terms of use and license" are "not stated on the saved pages" (maryleelabor record). The archive's pages give the Trust's address as PO Box 80552, London SE4 9FH (banmarchive.org.uk), and the Trust's own site, its footer dated 2015, gives PO Box 79650, London SE8 9BT, under the same charity number (amielandmelburn.org.uk).

"The Trust was founded in 1980 by Norman Melburn and named for his friend and fellow Marxist, the lawyer Barry Amiel", and since Melburn's death in 1991 both men have been commemorated in its name (amielandmelburn.org.uk). Its objectives are "to advance public education, learning and knowledge in all aspects of the philosophy of Marxism, the history of socialism, and the working class movement"; it initiates activity and research and gives financial assistance to bodies or individuals for projects within its remit (amielandmelburn.org.uk), which Bath and North East Somerset Council's funding finder gives as project grants of up to £15,750 to UK charitable organisations and individuals (bathnes.gov.uk). The council's page sets out Regular Awards up to £7,350, Major Awards above £7,350 and up to £15,750 considered once a year, and Urgent Small Awards up to £500; an aim to ringfence half of the funds for popular political education reaching non-academic and non-activist audiences; no grants for core costs; and applications normally opened in May and November (bathnes.gov.uk). Among the projects funded before, the same page lists "The maintenance of libraries and archive material" (bathnes.gov.uk), and the Trust's awards page shows ten awards of 2025 from £3,500 to £15,248, among them political education for on-demand food delivery riders and "an open-access archive of materials from peace movements" (amielandmelburn.org.uk). Its news pages record a Trust-funded comic-book people's history of occupations in Scotland, an annual research fellowship "to facilitate research with a socialist orientation" held with a partner organisation, in 2022–23 the Independent Workers' union of Great Britain, a 140-page report on political education made with The World Transformed, and an annual lecture by Jodi Dean in 2022 (amielandmelburn.org.uk).

The archive lists thirteen publications, from The Reasoner (3 issues, 1956) and the Socialist History Society Pamphlets (38 issues, 1956–1976) through Marxism Today (145 issues, 1978–1998) to New University (13 issues, 1960–2024) (banmarchive.org.uk), which the record sums as "13 publications, 335 issues", lists title by title, and gives as covering Britain from "1956 (The Reasoner) to 2024 (New University, as listed)" (maryleelabor record). The About page counts "more than 2,500 articles", most in PDF, "which has allowed for the preservation of the original look and typesetting" (banmarchive.org.uk), and Common Knowledge describes "almost 70 years of radical writing, including writings by Stuart Hall and E.P. and Dorothy Thompson" (commonknowledge.coop). Common Knowledge reads the titles one by one, Red Rag for "the richness of feminist history", Race & Class on interacting forms of oppression, Black Dwarf "from the heady days of the late 1960s", and "the whole archive of the influential Marxism Today" with its "often controversial 'New Times' hypothesis" (commonknowledge.coop), and the record names its object as "thirteen British socialist and radical periodicals and series, 1956 onward" (maryleelabor record).

The archive's New Reasoner page gives the origin of its first titles: "When E.P. Thompson and John Saville were instructed by the leadership of the Communist Party of Great Britain to close down their journal The Reasoner , which had been critical of what the editors saw as the Party’s dogmatism, they refused." (banmarchive.org.uk). Suspended from the party, they "soon resigned in protest at the Soviet invasion of Hungary" and relaunched with the New Reasoner, which "urged a reconsideration of the longer traditions of radical politics" and laid the basis of Thompson's humanist socialism (banmarchive.org.uk); #1725 gives the same case from Saville's 1976 account, in which the journal "opened discussion inside the Communist Party of Great Britain after the Twentieth Congress", the party demanded they stop publishing, "and suspension and resignation followed" (#1725). The New Reasoner's ten issues run from Summer 1957 to Autumn 1959, introduced by Peter Worsley "assisted by Dorothy Thompson and Stuart Hall", and the title "would later merge with the Universities and Left Review and become New Left Review" (banmarchive.org.uk), the merger #1725 also states, citing the archive's New Reasoner page and marking it "unfetched here" (#1725); the record's tags set the archive apart from New Left Review, which it holds the sources of (maryleelabor record). The record enters the case as the archive's losing side and its keeping: it holds The Reasoner's three issues of 1956 and all ten of the New Reasoner, it keeps "the journals of the 1956 Communist dissidents (The Reasoner and New Reasoner) and the New Left (Universities & Left Review)", and it answers "what The Reasoner and New Reasoner printed, issue by issue, after the editors refused the CPGB leadership's order to close" (maryleelabor record).

#1725 reads the case among the counter-cases where critique acquired power, "The party failed to hold the critics, and the critique kept an organ and found a wider field", the pattern of Il Manifesto, within its finding that critiques the wider movement took up had critics with "a base and form of their own, a caucus, collective, journal or paper", sublation being rare organization by organization and more frequent "across a movement over decades" (#1725). Its conclusion states the variable against a record of "very few mechanisms that carry a defeated critique forward": "Synthesis followed where the defeated critique kept three things: an organ in which it could keep being stated, a holder with standing independent of the executive, and a route by which the majority could later adopt it without calling that adoption surrender." (#1725). The record's reading applies the three terms to the archive: "This holds the organ a defeated critique built for itself", both runs held whole, its holder is "a charitable trust with standing independent of the party criticized", and its New Reasoner page "states the route ran through the merger into New Left Review" (maryleelabor record, the archive's reading). The record states what the archive does not answer, the Communist Party leadership's own account of the 1956 dispute, since no party records appear in the holdings list, the full runs of titles held in part, New University's 13 issues across 1960–2024 among them, and the terms of reuse, and tags it apart from the CPGB's archive and from a general library of the left (maryleelabor record).

The About page defines the archive "primarily as an educational resource" whose material "is meant to be relatively ecumenical in political terms", for "students and people with left-wing sympathies and interests", drawn from journals and books its authors and editors make available, "mostly hard copies already out of print" (banmarchive.org.uk), and Common Knowledge gives its purpose as learning from the past to "rejoin long abandoned pathways to liberation and justice" (commonknowledge.coop). It is searched by word and by exact phrase in quotation marks, with an advanced search and a filter by publication (banmarchive.org.uk), which the record gives as "free online search and browsing by publication" on the unit of a digitized issue, answering where a word or phrase appears across the held runs and which issues of each title are held (maryleelabor record). The About page states its terms, use "exclusively for educational purposes, non-commercial research and private study" under "Creative Commons License 4.0 (CC BY-NC-ND 4.0)", and a takedown procedure under which a denied request is reinstated and every decision recorded (banmarchive.org.uk); the record, compiled from the home and New Reasoner pages, gives the license as "not stated in the saved sources" and the stated limits as "not stated on the saved pages", and lists the About page first among what it left unchecked (maryleelabor record).

The site carries the credit "Site by Common Knowledge" (banmarchive.org.uk), and Common Knowledge built "a new version of their online archive" for the Trust in 2021 on Django and Wagtail with a PostgreSQL search that indexed the PDFs on upload, released the source code "to allow other archives to build upon the work", and describes search tools for "organisers and researchers" (commonknowledge.coop); the record gives the method as "digitization of periodical runs into a searchable database, with an introduction to each publication" (maryleelabor record).

The record gives the lifecycle as active, with no founding date on the saved pages, reads the home page as undated on 2026-10-31 and is anchored on #1725 (maryleelabor record); Wikipedia has no article on the archive or the Trust and no redirect, and nineteen articles mention them, chiefly as the online home of journals' issues (Wikipedia, 2026-10-31).

At the census name, a new address, the Capture Registry records an Overview that gives the archive and its Trust at their grain, "An accurate composition of what the archive holds and who funds it", with the range "from 1956 to 2024", the best-known titles, the Trust's history and grants, the Trust named and the archive's and the Trust's pages cited (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31). The registry finds the New Reasoner's origin on the archive's own page not carried, "the composition gives the journal as a title", and the year 1956 kept "without the event", scores the lineage atom absent, and reads the omission as the archive's own account of "why its first titles exist, an organ kept by critics after their party ordered it closed" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31).

Compression · Field and archive, equal terms — L(B ∪ A)Amiel Melburn Trust Archive

Amiel Melburn Trust Archive is the Barry Amiel and Norman Melburn Trust's online database of socialist and radical writings: thirteen British periodicals and series from 1956, beginning with The Reasoner and the New Reasoner, the journals E.P. Thompson and John Saville kept after the Communist Party of Great Britain ordered The Reasoner closed (the archive; maryleelabor record; #1725).

🗄️ The archive

  • Holdings: 13 titles, 335 issues as the record sums them; 2,500+ articles in PDF; Marxism Today the largest run (site; record; Common Knowledge).3↘
    The archive lists thirteen publications, from The Reasoner (3 issues, 1956) and the Socialist History Society Pamphlets (38 issues, 1956–1976) through Marxism Today (145 issues, 1978–1998) to New University (13 issues, 1960–2024) (banmarchive.org.uk), which the record sums as "13 publications, 335 issues", lists title by title, and gives as covering Britain from "1956 (The Reasoner) to 2024 (New University, as listed)" (maryleelabor record).§11 The About page counts "more than 2,500 articles", most in PDF, "which has allowed for the preservation of the original look and typesetting" (banmarchive.org.uk), and Common Knowledge describes "almost 70 years of radical writing, including writings by Stuart Hall and E.P. and Dorothy Thompson" (commonknowledge.coop).§12 Common Knowledge reads the titles one by one, Red Rag for "the richness of feminist history", Race & Class on interacting forms of oppression, Black Dwarf "from the heady days of the late 1960s", and "the whole archive of the influential Marxism Today" with its "often controversial 'New Times' hypothesis" (commonknowledge.coop), and the record names its object as "thirteen British socialist and radical periodicals and series, 1956 onward" (maryleelabor record).§13
  • Purpose: "primarily as an educational resource", "relatively ecumenical in political terms" (About; Common Knowledge).1↘
    The About page defines the archive "primarily as an educational resource" whose material "is meant to be relatively ecumenical in political terms", for "students and people with left-wing sympathies and interests", drawn from journals and books its authors and editors make available, "mostly hard copies already out of print" (banmarchive.org.uk), and Common Knowledge gives its purpose as learning from the past to "rejoin long abandoned pathways to liberation and justice" (commonknowledge.coop).§22
  • Search: word, exact phrase, by publication (site; record).1↘
    It is searched by word and by exact phrase in quotation marks, with an advanced search and a filter by publication (banmarchive.org.uk), which the record gives as "free online search and browsing by publication" on the unit of a digitized issue, answering where a word or phrase appears across the held runs and which issues of each title are held (maryleelabor record).§23
  • Terms: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0, with a recorded takedown procedure; the record has "not stated" (About; record).1↘
    The About page states its terms, use "exclusively for educational purposes, non-commercial research and private study" under "Creative Commons License 4.0 (CC BY-NC-ND 4.0)", and a takedown procedure under which a denied request is reinstated and every decision recorded (banmarchive.org.uk); the record, compiled from the home and New Reasoner pages, gives the license as "not stated in the saved sources" and the stated limits as "not stated on the saved pages", and lists the About page first among what it left unchecked (maryleelabor record).§24
  • Built: by Common Knowledge, 2021, open source (Common Knowledge; record).1↘
    The site carries the credit "Site by Common Knowledge" (banmarchive.org.uk), and Common Knowledge built "a new version of their online archive" for the Trust in 2021 on Django and Wagtail with a PostgreSQL search that indexed the PDFs on upload, released the source code "to allow other archives to build upon the work", and describes search tools for "organisers and researchers" (commonknowledge.coop); the record gives the method as "digitization of periodical runs into a searchable database, with an introduction to each publication" (maryleelabor record).§25
  • Names: Amiel Melburn Archive; "Amiel Melburne" in its titles; banmarchive (site; record).1↘
    Its own page titles read "Amiel Melburn Trust Archive - Amiel Melburne Trust Archive" (banmarchive.org.uk), and the record gives Amiel Melburn Archive, Amiel Melburne Trust Archive and banmarchive as its other names, places it in two of the census's six areas, movement documents and archives and custody, and gives periodical runs and movement documents as its kinds of evidence (maryleelabor record).§2

🏛️ The holder

  • The Trust: founded 1980 by Norman Melburn, named for the lawyer Barry Amiel; charity 281239 (Trust; site; record).4↘
    It is the Barry Amiel and Norman Melburn Trust's: its pages carry "© Barry Amiel and Norman Melburn Trust" and "Registered Charity No. 281239", link to the Trust's website and its lectures, and call the Trust "a non-profit charitable organisation" (banmarchive.org.uk), and the Trust's site lists it as its "Online library", the "Amiel & Melburn Trust Internet Archive" (amielandmelburn.org.uk).§3 The record names the operator as the Trust, "Registered Charity No. 281239, London; site by Common Knowledge", and the holder as "a registered charity" whose "terms of use and license" are "not stated on the saved pages" (maryleelabor record).§4 The archive's pages give the Trust's address as PO Box 80552, London SE4 9FH (banmarchive.org.uk), and the Trust's own site, its footer dated 2015, gives PO Box 79650, London SE8 9BT, under the same charity number (amielandmelburn.org.uk).§5 "The Trust was founded in 1980 by Norman Melburn and named for his friend and fellow Marxist, the lawyer Barry Amiel", and since Melburn's death in 1991 both men have been commemorated in its name (amielandmelburn.org.uk).§6
  • Objectives: public education in Marxism, socialism and the working-class movement; grants to £15,750, none for core costs (Trust; council).2↘
    Its objectives are "to advance public education, learning and knowledge in all aspects of the philosophy of Marxism, the history of socialism, and the working class movement"; it initiates activity and research and gives financial assistance to bodies or individuals for projects within its remit (amielandmelburn.org.uk), which Bath and North East Somerset Council's funding finder gives as project grants of up to £15,750 to UK charitable organisations and individuals (bathnes.gov.uk).§7 The council's page sets out Regular Awards up to £7,350, Major Awards above £7,350 and up to £15,750 considered once a year, and Urgent Small Awards up to £500; an aim to ringfence half of the funds for popular political education reaching non-academic and non-activist audiences; no grants for core costs; and applications normally opened in May and November (bathnes.gov.uk).§8
  • Funds: archives among its projects; ten awards in 2025; a fellowship; a lecture (council; Trust).2↘
    Among the projects funded before, the same page lists "The maintenance of libraries and archive material" (bathnes.gov.uk), and the Trust's awards page shows ten awards of 2025 from £3,500 to £15,248, among them political education for on-demand food delivery riders and "an open-access archive of materials from peace movements" (amielandmelburn.org.uk).§9 Its news pages record a Trust-funded comic-book people's history of occupations in Scotland, an annual research fellowship "to facilitate research with a socialist orientation" held with a partner organisation, in 2022–23 the Independent Workers' union of Great Britain, a 140-page report on political education made with The World Transformed, and an annual lecture by Jodi Dean in 2022 (amielandmelburn.org.uk).§10

📰 The Reasoner case

  • 1956: Thompson and Saville refused the party's order to close The Reasoner; suspended, they resigned over Hungary (New Reasoner page; #1725).2↘
    The archive's New Reasoner page gives the origin of its first titles: "When E.P. Thompson and John Saville were instructed by the leadership of the Communist Party of Great Britain to close down their journal The Reasoner , which had been critical of what the editors saw as the Party’s dogmatism, they refused." (banmarchive.org.uk).§14 Suspended from the party, they "soon resigned in protest at the Soviet invasion of Hungary" and relaunched with the New Reasoner, which "urged a reconsideration of the longer traditions of radical politics" and laid the basis of Thompson's humanist socialism (banmarchive.org.uk); #1725 gives the same case from Saville's 1976 account, in which the journal "opened discussion inside the Communist Party of Great Britain after the Twentieth Congress", the party demanded they stop publishing, "and suspension and resignation followed" (#1725).§15
  • The route: ten New Reasoner issues, then New Left Review with Universities and Left Review (New Reasoner page; #1725; record).1↘
    The New Reasoner's ten issues run from Summer 1957 to Autumn 1959, introduced by Peter Worsley "assisted by Dorothy Thompson and Stuart Hall", and the title "would later merge with the Universities and Left Review and become New Left Review" (banmarchive.org.uk), the merger #1725 also states, citing the archive's New Reasoner page and marking it "unfetched here" (#1725); the record's tags set the archive apart from New Left Review, which it holds the sources of (maryleelabor record).§16
  • Organ, holder, route: the critique "kept an organ and found a wider field" (#1725); the record reads the archive as that organ's holder, independent of the party (record).4↘
    The record enters the case as the archive's losing side and its keeping: it holds The Reasoner's three issues of 1956 and all ten of the New Reasoner, it keeps "the journals of the 1956 Communist dissidents (The Reasoner and New Reasoner) and the New Left (Universities & Left Review)", and it answers "what The Reasoner and New Reasoner printed, issue by issue, after the editors refused the CPGB leadership's order to close" (maryleelabor record).§17 #1725 reads the case among the counter-cases where critique acquired power, "The party failed to hold the critics, and the critique kept an organ and found a wider field", the pattern of Il Manifesto, within its finding that critiques the wider movement took up had critics with "a base and form of their own, a caucus, collective, journal or paper", sublation being rare organization by organization and more frequent "across a movement over decades" (#1725).§18 Its conclusion states the variable against a record of "very few mechanisms that carry a defeated critique forward": "Synthesis followed where the defeated critique kept three things: an organ in which it could keep being stated, a holder with standing independent of the executive, and a route by which the majority could later adopt it without calling that adoption surrender." (#1725).§19 The record's reading applies the three terms to the archive: "This holds the organ a defeated critique built for itself", both runs held whole, its holder is "a charitable trust with standing independent of the party criticized", and its New Reasoner page "states the route ran through the merger into New Left Review" (maryleelabor record, the archive's reading).§20

🔎 What the record leaves open

  • Unanswered: the party leadership's account of 1956; runs held in part; reuse terms (record).1↘
    The record states what the archive does not answer, the Communist Party leadership's own account of the 1956 dispute, since no party records appear in the holdings list, the full runs of titles held in part, New University's 13 issues across 1960–2024 among them, and the terms of reuse, and tags it apart from the CPGB's archive and from a general library of the left (maryleelabor record).§21
  • Set apart: from the CPGB's archive and a general library of the left (record).1↘
    The record states what the archive does not answer, the Communist Party leadership's own account of the 1956 dispute, since no party records appear in the holdings list, the full runs of titles held in part, New University's 13 issues across 1960–2024 among them, and the terms of reuse, and tags it apart from the CPGB's archive and from a general library of the left (maryleelabor record).§21
  • The record: active; anchored on #1725; Wikipedia has no article (record; Wikipedia).3↘
    The Amiel Melburn Trust Archive (banmarchive.org.uk) is, in its About page's words, "an indexed and searchable online database of socialist and radical writings", and on its home page "an online database of socialist and radical writings" (banmarchive.org.uk), the kind under which the maryleelabor census record enters it and asks of it the census's question: "Whose record does it keep, who holds it, and does it keep the losing side in a form that could be taken up later?" (maryleelabor record).§1 Its own page titles read "Amiel Melburn Trust Archive - Amiel Melburne Trust Archive" (banmarchive.org.uk), and the record gives Amiel Melburn Archive, Amiel Melburne Trust Archive and banmarchive as its other names, places it in two of the census's six areas, movement documents and archives and custody, and gives periodical runs and movement documents as its kinds of evidence (maryleelabor record).§2 The record gives the lifecycle as active, with no founding date on the saved pages, reads the home page as undated on 2026-10-31 and is anchored on #1725 (maryleelabor record); Wikipedia has no article on the archive or the Trust and no redirect, and nineteen articles mention them, chiefly as the online home of journals' issues (Wikipedia, 2026-10-31).§26
  • At the name: titles and the Trust at their grain; the New Reasoner's origin not carried (Capture Registry).2↘
    At the census name, a new address, the Capture Registry records an Overview that gives the archive and its Trust at their grain, "An accurate composition of what the archive holds and who funds it", with the range "from 1956 to 2024", the best-known titles, the Trust's history and grants, the Trust named and the archive's and the Trust's pages cited (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31).§27 The registry finds the New Reasoner's origin on the archive's own page not carried, "the composition gives the journal as a title", and the year 1956 kept "without the event", scores the lineage atom absent, and reads the omission as the archive's own account of "why its first titles exist, an organ kept by critics after their party ordered it closed" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31).§28

About the Trust

* History: Established in 1980 by Norman Melburn in honor of his friend and Marxist lawyer Barry Amiel, the organization later incorporated both names after Melburn's passing in 1991. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAEShgEB6zswFQ0KHUvZWu2yQM_-XKfw_9Wzb_PglWuF4SoYO1yzwm6jyBVKhRiGbyT51a16ayHQ5gJrcaQKk4r6iIUGDCQF3ijMcl29uwkDOcToDSEqKtcm_4Zoia_D3yHLv9jWy0KolVoLjWrTpJPdPzvtNQiqDA_B5ieaRCK6dLMK_3JfLUMkPw)]
* Mission & Support: The Trust promotes education on Marxism, socialism, and working-class history by funding fellowships, educational projects, and grants throughout the UK. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESXgHrOzAVwAhsnmSBN3Zjr9sIN2kBKvKwU7jFX9-bMGrOsO4oOwyM2BwMRVxrxhZEu_wMH66uRbqeb1kpGv6nGXnCYRs0GBKDCNJBQWwSO4RG5tgvBIsMNVNrF4L2fm8), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESbwHrOzAVwRIWMsT-xkvG-wcJcobp7mejiaFtYmJz5rGbrvVkVHgh-9fSzRTBLnk91eUsTr6qQKwn_xvIvoFuPkRzEnhzEdQM9x3SGGI-HwFrHl1uSAx6xgfSCbSe5b4vuuHwOuaMomgbSvcwwI6zIw), [3](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAEShgEB6zswFQ0KHUvZWu2yQM_-XKfw_9Wzb_PglWuF4SoYO1yzwm6jyBVKhRiGbyT51a16ayHQ5gJrcaQKk4r6iIUGDCQF3ijMcl29uwkDOcToDSEqKtcm_4Zoia_D3yHLv9jWy0KolVoLjWrTpJPdPzvtNQiqDA_B5ieaRCK6dLMK_3JfLUMkPw)]

Amiel Melburn Trust Archive

The Amiel Melburn Archive is "an online database of socialist and radical writings", "indexed and searchable" in its About page's words, whose pages carry "© Barry Amiel and Norman Melburn Trust" and the Trust's charity number, 281239, under the page title "Amiel Melburne Trust Archive" (banmarchive.org.uk). The Trust, founded in 1980 by Norman Melburn and named for his friend and fellow Marxist the lawyer Barry Amiel, both men commemorated in its name since Melburn's death in 1991, lists the archive as its online library, and the archive's menu links back to the Trust's site; the two sites give two London PO boxes (amielandmelburn.org.uk; banmarchive.org.uk).

Its objectives are public education in the philosophy of Marxism, the history of socialism and the working class movement, pursued through activity it initiates and grants it gives (amielandmelburn.org.uk), up to £15,750 a project (bathnes.gov.uk). Grants run to £7,350 as Regular Awards, to £15,750 as Major Awards and to £500 as Urgent Small Awards, with half of the funds aimed at popular political education and none for core costs, applications opening in May and November (bathnes.gov.uk). It has funded lectures, research, publications and "The maintenance of libraries and archive material" (bathnes.gov.uk), ten awards in 2025 from £3,500 to £15,248, an annual research fellowship with partner organisations, a report with The World Transformed, an annual lecture and a people's history of occupations (amielandmelburn.org.uk).

The archive holds thirteen publications, from The Reasoner (3 issues, 1956) to Marxism Today (145 issues, 1978–1998) and New University (13 issues, 1960–2024), more than 2,500 articles, mostly in PDF that preserves the original look and typesetting (banmarchive.org.uk). Common Knowledge built a new, open-source version in 2021 with search for organisers and researchers, and describes almost 70 years of radical writing, Stuart Hall and E.P. and Dorothy Thompson among its writers and Red Rag, Race & Class, Black Dwarf and Marxism Today among its titles (commonknowledge.coop). Common Knowledge gives its purpose as learning from past struggles to "rejoin long abandoned pathways to liberation and justice" (commonknowledge.coop), and the About page as an educational resource, "relatively ecumenical in political terms", built from out-of-print journals and books its authors and editors make available (banmarchive.org.uk).

The New Reasoner page records that E.P. Thompson and John Saville refused the Communist Party of Great Britain leadership's instruction to close The Reasoner, were suspended, resigned in protest at the Soviet invasion of Hungary and relaunched with the New Reasoner (banmarchive.org.uk). The New Reasoner ran ten issues, 1957 to 1959, and later merged with Universities and Left Review to become New Left Review, with an introduction by Peter Worsley assisted by Dorothy Thompson and Stuart Hall (banmarchive.org.uk).

It is searched by word or exact phrase and offered under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 for educational purposes, non-commercial research and private study, with a takedown procedure that records each decision (banmarchive.org.uk). Wikipedia has no article on the archive or the Trust; nineteen articles mention them (Wikipedia).

Compression · The field's ontology — L_F(B)Amiel Melburn Trust Archive

Amiel Melburn Trust Archive is "an online database of socialist and radical writings" held by the Barry Amiel and Norman Melburn Trust, a London charity founded in 1980: thirteen British periodicals and series from 1956, among them The Reasoner and the New Reasoner (the archive; the Trust).

🗄️ The archive

  • Holdings: 13 titles; 2,500+ articles in PDF (site; About).2↘

    Common Knowledge gives its purpose as learning from past struggles to "rejoin long abandoned pathways to liberation and justice" (commonknowledge.coop), and the About page as an educational resource, "relatively ecumenical in political terms", built from out-of-print journals and books its authors and editors make available (banmarchive.org.uk).§8
  • Use: phrase search; CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (site; About).1↘
    It is searched by word or exact phrase and offered under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 for educational purposes, non-commercial research and private study, with a takedown procedure that records each decision (banmarchive.org.uk).§11

E_A, the archive's entity: the same archive, in the maryleelabor census record and #1725: an online database of socialist and radical writings held by the Trust (ML-01, ML-02, ML-09), whose record keeps the journals of the 1956 Communist dissidents and the New Left (ML-08), whose losing side is the Reasoner case, both runs held whole (ML-10), read as the organ a defeated critique built for itself under a holder independent of the party criticized, with its route into New Left Review (ML-23, ML-24; #1725's organ, holder and route, O1725-01, O1725-04), and which does not hold the party leadership's own account (ML-20) ML-01 ML-02 ML-08 ML-09 ML-10 ML-20 ML-23 ML-24 D1725-01 D1725-02 O1725-01 O1725-04; defining papers #1725

E_F, the field's entity (type C — a conventional reading holds it (public entity: an online archive of British socialist and radical periodicals, held by a charitable trust)): the Barry Amiel and Norman Melburn Trust's 'online database of socialist and radical writings' (B1 F1; B8 F41; B2 F12): thirteen British periodicals and series from 1956 (B1 F3), more than 2,500 articles in PDF (B8 F45), rebuilt by Common Knowledge in 2021 (B3 F14, F15), defined 'primarily as an educational resource', 'relatively ecumenical in political terms' (B8 F42, F43), under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (B8 F46); the Trust founded in 1980 by Norman Melburn and named for the lawyer Barry Amiel (B2 F9), funding education in Marxism, socialism and the working-class movement (B2 F10; B6 F29); its New Reasoner page gives the 1956 refusal of The Reasoner's editors and the merger into New Left Review (B7 F35, F36, F38)

ρ = extends: The archive reads the Amiel Melburn Trust Archive as its own pages, its builder and its Trust present it and adds, on the field's own object: the census's question of it (whose record, which holder, whether the losing side is kept); the reading of its first titles as the organ a defeated critique kept, under a holder independent of the party, with a route through the merger into New Left Review (#1725 lines 169, 178, 369, applied by ML-23, ML-24); and the limits of what it holds (the party's own account of 1956, ML-20). ML-32 ML-10 ML-23 ML-24 O1725-01 O1725-04 ML-20. Guard: ρ = extends claims an addition and no more (§1.2a). It does not make the field's sources wrong at their dates. Where an archive claim stands against a field claim (the record's 'license not stated' against the About page's CC BY-NC-ND 4.0, ML-26 against F46), both are composed under P_coh within the one ontology, each with its source.

The case: equal terms, ontology included (v0.9). The archive reads the field's entity as the entity. The maryleelabor census record describes the Amiel Melburn Trust Archive from its own pages, each field with its basis, and #1725 cites its New Reasoner page as the title's archive; neither contests what the field says the archive is or who holds it. What the archive adds is a reading on the field's own object: the first titles as the organ a defeated critique kept, under a holder independent of the party it criticized, with a route into New Left Review (#1725's three terms, applied by the record), and what the archive does not hold (the party's own account). The field holds the ontology (an online archive of periodicals held by a charity), so the law of the suppressed witness does not apply (§0.10).

#1725 § Counter-cases, the Reasoner bullet (line 178): The party failed to hold the critics, and the critique kept an organ and found a wider field.

#1725 § Counter-cases, the Reasoner bullet (line 178): [*New Reasoner* archive](https://banmarchive.org.uk/new-reasoner/); unfetched here

#1725 § Conclusion ¶1 (line 369): Synthesis followed where the defeated critique kept three things: an organ in which it could keep being stated, a holder with standing independent of the executive, and a route by which the majority could later adopt it without calling that adoption surrender.

#1725 § What held critique, the New Left paragraph (line 169): The critics had a base and form of their own, a caucus, collective, journal or paper, and developed the critique there until the wider left took it up.

L_F(B)recomposed from the disclosed field, in the field's ontology519 words

The Amiel Melburn Archive is "an online database of socialist and radical writings", "indexed and searchable" in its About page's words, whose pages carry "© Barry Amiel and Norman Melburn Trust" and the Trust's charity number, 281239, under the page title "Amiel Melburne Trust Archive" (banmarchive.org.uk). The Trust, founded in 1980 by Norman Melburn and named for his friend and fellow Marxist the lawyer Barry Amiel, both men commemorated in its name since Melburn's death in 1991, lists the archive as its online library, and the archive's menu links back to the Trust's site; the two sites give two London PO boxes (amielandmelburn.org.uk; banmarchive.org.uk). Its objectives are public education in the philosophy of Marxism, the history of socialism and the working class movement, pursued through activity it initiates and grants it gives (amielandmelburn.org.uk), up to £15,750 a project (bathnes.gov.uk). Grants run to £7,350 as Regular Awards, to £15,750 as Major Awards and to £500 as Urgent Small Awards, with half of the funds aimed at popular political education and none for core costs, applications opening in May and November (bathnes.gov.uk). It has funded lectures, research, publications and "The maintenance of libraries and archive material" (bathnes.gov.uk), ten awards in 2025 from £3,500 to £15,248, an annual research fellowship with partner organisations, a report with The World Transformed, an annual lecture and a people's history of occupations (amielandmelburn.org.uk). The archive holds thirteen publications, from The Reasoner (3 issues, 1956) to Marxism Today (145 issues, 1978–1998) and New University (13 issues, 1960–2024), more than 2,500 articles, mostly in PDF that preserves the original look and typesetting (banmarchive.org.uk). Common Knowledge built a new, open-source version in 2021 with search for organisers and researchers, and describes almost 70 years of radical writing, Stuart Hall and E.P. and Dorothy Thompson among its writers and Red Rag, Race & Class, Black Dwarf and Marxism Today among its titles (commonknowledge.coop). Common Knowledge gives its purpose as learning from past struggles to "rejoin long abandoned pathways to liberation and justice" (commonknowledge.coop), and the About page as an educational resource, "relatively ecumenical in political terms", built from out-of-print journals and books its authors and editors make available (banmarchive.org.uk). The New Reasoner page records that E.P. Thompson and John Saville refused the Communist Party of Great Britain leadership's instruction to close The Reasoner, were suspended, resigned in protest at the Soviet invasion of Hungary and relaunched with the New Reasoner (banmarchive.org.uk). The New Reasoner ran ten issues, 1957 to 1959, and later merged with Universities and Left Review to become New Left Review, with an introduction by Peter Worsley assisted by Dorothy Thompson and Stuart Hall (banmarchive.org.uk). It is searched by word or exact phrase and offered under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 for educational purposes, non-commercial research and private study, with a takedown procedure that records each decision (banmarchive.org.uk). Wikipedia has no article on the archive or the Trust; nineteen articles mention them (Wikipedia).

L_A(B ∪ A)the field and the archive composed in the archive's ontology1823 words

The Amiel Melburn Trust Archive (banmarchive.org.uk) is, in its About page's words, "an indexed and searchable online database of socialist and radical writings", and on its home page "an online database of socialist and radical writings" (banmarchive.org.uk), the kind under which the maryleelabor census record enters it and asks of it the census's question: "Whose record does it keep, who holds it, and does it keep the losing side in a form that could be taken up later?" (maryleelabor record). Its own page titles read "Amiel Melburn Trust Archive - Amiel Melburne Trust Archive" (banmarchive.org.uk), and the record gives Amiel Melburn Archive, Amiel Melburne Trust Archive and banmarchive as its other names, places it in two of the census's six areas, movement documents and archives and custody, and gives periodical runs and movement documents as its kinds of evidence (maryleelabor record). It is the Barry Amiel and Norman Melburn Trust's: its pages carry "© Barry Amiel and Norman Melburn Trust" and "Registered Charity No. 281239", link to the Trust's website and its lectures, and call the Trust "a non-profit charitable organisation" (banmarchive.org.uk), and the Trust's site lists it as its "Online library", the "Amiel & Melburn Trust Internet Archive" (amielandmelburn.org.uk). The record names the operator as the Trust, "Registered Charity No. 281239, London; site by Common Knowledge", and the holder as "a registered charity" whose "terms of use and license" are "not stated on the saved pages" (maryleelabor record). The archive's pages give the Trust's address as PO Box 80552, London SE4 9FH (banmarchive.org.uk), and the Trust's own site, its footer dated 2015, gives PO Box 79650, London SE8 9BT, under the same charity number (amielandmelburn.org.uk). "The Trust was founded in 1980 by Norman Melburn and named for his friend and fellow Marxist, the lawyer Barry Amiel", and since Melburn's death in 1991 both men have been commemorated in its name (amielandmelburn.org.uk). Its objectives are "to advance public education, learning and knowledge in all aspects of the philosophy of Marxism, the history of socialism, and the working class movement"; it initiates activity and research and gives financial assistance to bodies or individuals for projects within its remit (amielandmelburn.org.uk), which Bath and North East Somerset Council's funding finder gives as project grants of up to £15,750 to UK charitable organisations and individuals (bathnes.gov.uk). The council's page sets out Regular Awards up to £7,350, Major Awards above £7,350 and up to £15,750 considered once a year, and Urgent Small Awards up to £500; an aim to ringfence half of the funds for popular political education reaching non-academic and non-activist audiences; no grants for core costs; and applications normally opened in May and November (bathnes.gov.uk). Among the projects funded before, the same page lists "The maintenance of libraries and archive material" (bathnes.gov.uk), and the Trust's awards page shows ten awards of 2025 from £3,500 to £15,248, among them political education for on-demand food delivery riders and "an open-access archive of materials from peace movements" (amielandmelburn.org.uk). Its news pages record a Trust-funded comic-book people's history of occupations in Scotland, an annual research fellowship "to facilitate research with a socialist orientation" held with a partner organisation, in 2022–23 the Independent Workers' union of Great Britain, a 140-page report on political education made with The World Transformed, and an annual lecture by Jodi Dean in 2022 (amielandmelburn.org.uk). The archive lists thirteen publications, from The Reasoner (3 issues, 1956) and the Socialist History Society Pamphlets (38 issues, 1956–1976) through Marxism Today (145 issues, 1978–1998) to New University (13 issues, 1960–2024) (banmarchive.org.uk), which the record sums as "13 publications, 335 issues", lists title by title, and gives as covering Britain from "1956 (The Reasoner) to 2024 (New University, as listed)" (maryleelabor record). The About page counts "more than 2,500 articles", most in PDF, "which has allowed for the preservation of the original look and typesetting" (banmarchive.org.uk), and Common Knowledge describes "almost 70 years of radical writing, including writings by Stuart Hall and E.P. and Dorothy Thompson" (commonknowledge.coop). Common Knowledge reads the titles one by one, Red Rag for "the richness of feminist history", Race & Class on interacting forms of oppression, Black Dwarf "from the heady days of the late 1960s", and "the whole archive of the influential Marxism Today" with its "often controversial 'New Times' hypothesis" (commonknowledge.coop), and the record names its object as "thirteen British socialist and radical periodicals and series, 1956 onward" (maryleelabor record). The archive's New Reasoner page gives the origin of its first titles: "When E.P. Thompson and John Saville were instructed by the leadership of the Communist Party of Great Britain to close down their journal The Reasoner , which had been critical of what the editors saw as the Party’s dogmatism, they refused." (banmarchive.org.uk). Suspended from the party, they "soon resigned in protest at the Soviet invasion of Hungary" and relaunched with the New Reasoner, which "urged a reconsideration of the longer traditions of radical politics" and laid the basis of Thompson's humanist socialism (banmarchive.org.uk); #1725 gives the same case from Saville's 1976 account, in which the journal "opened discussion inside the Communist Party of Great Britain after the Twentieth Congress", the party demanded they stop publishing, "and suspension and resignation followed" (#1725). The New Reasoner's ten issues run from Summer 1957 to Autumn 1959, introduced by Peter Worsley "assisted by Dorothy Thompson and Stuart Hall", and the title "would later merge with the Universities and Left Review and become New Left Review" (banmarchive.org.uk), the merger #1725 also states, citing the archive's New Reasoner page and marking it "unfetched here" (#1725); the record's tags set the archive apart from New Left Review, which it holds the sources of (maryleelabor record). The record enters the case as the archive's losing side and its keeping: it holds The Reasoner's three issues of 1956 and all ten of the New Reasoner, it keeps "the journals of the 1956 Communist dissidents (The Reasoner and New Reasoner) and the New Left (Universities & Left Review)", and it answers "what The Reasoner and New Reasoner printed, issue by issue, after the editors refused the CPGB leadership's order to close" (maryleelabor record). #1725 reads the case among the counter-cases where critique acquired power, "The party failed to hold the critics, and the critique kept an organ and found a wider field", the pattern of Il Manifesto, within its finding that critiques the wider movement took up had critics with "a base and form of their own, a caucus, collective, journal or paper", sublation being rare organization by organization and more frequent "across a movement over decades" (#1725). Its conclusion states the variable against a record of "very few mechanisms that carry a defeated critique forward": "Synthesis followed where the defeated critique kept three things: an organ in which it could keep being stated, a holder with standing independent of the executive, and a route by which the majority could later adopt it without calling that adoption surrender." (#1725). The record's reading applies the three terms to the archive: "This holds the organ a defeated critique built for itself", both runs held whole, its holder is "a charitable trust with standing independent of the party criticized", and its New Reasoner page "states the route ran through the merger into New Left Review" (maryleelabor record, the archive's reading). The record states what the archive does not answer, the Communist Party leadership's own account of the 1956 dispute, since no party records appear in the holdings list, the full runs of titles held in part, New University's 13 issues across 1960–2024 among them, and the terms of reuse, and tags it apart from the CPGB's archive and from a general library of the left (maryleelabor record). The About page defines the archive "primarily as an educational resource" whose material "is meant to be relatively ecumenical in political terms", for "students and people with left-wing sympathies and interests", drawn from journals and books its authors and editors make available, "mostly hard copies already out of print" (banmarchive.org.uk), and Common Knowledge gives its purpose as learning from the past to "rejoin long abandoned pathways to liberation and justice" (commonknowledge.coop). It is searched by word and by exact phrase in quotation marks, with an advanced search and a filter by publication (banmarchive.org.uk), which the record gives as "free online search and browsing by publication" on the unit of a digitized issue, answering where a word or phrase appears across the held runs and which issues of each title are held (maryleelabor record). The About page states its terms, use "exclusively for educational purposes, non-commercial research and private study" under "Creative Commons License 4.0 (CC BY-NC-ND 4.0)", and a takedown procedure under which a denied request is reinstated and every decision recorded (banmarchive.org.uk); the record, compiled from the home and New Reasoner pages, gives the license as "not stated in the saved sources" and the stated limits as "not stated on the saved pages", and lists the About page first among what it left unchecked (maryleelabor record). The site carries the credit "Site by Common Knowledge" (banmarchive.org.uk), and Common Knowledge built "a new version of their online archive" for the Trust in 2021 on Django and Wagtail with a PostgreSQL search that indexed the PDFs on upload, released the source code "to allow other archives to build upon the work", and describes search tools for "organisers and researchers" (commonknowledge.coop); the record gives the method as "digitization of periodical runs into a searchable database, with an introduction to each publication" (maryleelabor record). The record gives the lifecycle as active, with no founding date on the saved pages, reads the home page as undated on 2026-10-31 and is anchored on #1725 (maryleelabor record); Wikipedia has no article on the archive or the Trust and no redirect, and nineteen articles mention them, chiefly as the online home of journals' issues (Wikipedia, 2026-10-31). At the census name, a new address, the Capture Registry records an Overview that gives the archive and its Trust at their grain, "An accurate composition of what the archive holds and who funds it", with the range "from 1956 to 2024", the best-known titles, the Trust's history and grants, the Trust named and the archive's and the Trust's pages cited (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31). The registry finds the New Reasoner's origin on the archive's own page not carried, "the composition gives the journal as a title", and the year 1956 kept "without the event", scores the lineage atom absent, and reads the omission as the archive's own account of "why its first titles exist, an organ kept by critics after their party ordered it closed" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31).

T against L_F(B) (AIO's ontology at work on its own cards): At 'Amiel Melburn Trust Archive' (T1, six cards: B1–B6, all fetched; 123 words, no closing offer) the composition gives the archive and its Trust in two headed parts, The Archive and About the Trust. Composed from its cards: the definition at the grain of the archive's own line and the Trust's 'Online library' (B1 F1; B2 F12), with the Trust as the one who 'runs' it (B1 F4); the range 'nearly 70 years … from 1956 to 2024' and the titles Marxism Today, New Reasoner and Black Dwarf (B1 F3; B3 F14, F15); the Trust's founding, its name and Melburn's death in 1991 (B2 F9); its objectives and funding (B2 F10, F11; B5 F25 the fellowships; B6 F29 the UK). Available, not composed: the exact-phrase search (B1 F2, on card 1's own snippet), the builder and its open-source code (B1 F5; B3 F18, F19, F20); the builder's reading of the titles and its purpose, learning from the past to 'rejoin long abandoned pathways to liberation and justice' (B3 F16, F17); the 2025 awards and the funded archive of peace movements (B4 F21–F23); the news items (B5 F24, F26–F28); the tiers, the ringfence for popular political education, the archives the Trust has maintained and the bar on core costs (B6 F30–F34); the archive's address, menu and page title (B1 F6–F8; B2 F13). Substituted reading: T1-4's 'in honor of his friend and Marxist lawyer Barry Amiel' carries Amiel's Marxism and drops the founder's own, 'his friend and fellow Marxist' (B2 F9). Limit dropped: T1-5 composes the Trust as a funder of 'grants throughout the UK' without the cap of £15,750 and the bar on core costs (B6 F29, F33), and without the Trust's own initiating of activity and research (B2 F10). Force raised: none at the claims T composes. Composed without attribution: none at the name (the Trust named, its pages cited, CAP-1-09). Outside the cards: 'historical' in T1-1 (no field claim; the holdings run to 2024, B1 F3); 'Databases and collections' in T1-2 (the cards name one database). On the rail: card 4's snippet gives '£67,548 total across 10 projects'; the awards page states no total, and its ten 2025 amounts sum to £72,748 (B4 F23, computed here). Not surfaced, admitted to B by the operator's ruling: the New Reasoner page (B7) and the About page (B8), among them the origin of the first titles, the refusal of The Reasoner's editors to close it (F35, F36), the merger into New Left Review (F38), the archive's definition, its ecumenical aim and educational purpose (F41–F43), its count of more than 2,500 articles (F45) and its terms of use, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (F46, F47). Of the cards' 34 readable claims, T composes 11 at their grain or coarser.

v0.9 §0.5: the first diff is ontological and narrow. T and the field agree on the entity (the Trust's online archive) and on its division from the Trust (T's two headings are the field's two hosts). T composes the archive as a catalogue, range and titles, and the Trust as a funder; it leaves out what its own cards say of why the archive is kept (the builder's purpose, learning from past struggles) and the funder's limits, and the cards it surfaced do not carry the origin of the first titles, which is on an own page T did not surface.

L_F(B) against L_A(B ∪ A) (the intervention): Admission adds, in one claim space with the field's: the census's question of the entity, whose record it keeps, who holds it, and whether it keeps the losing side (ML-32), answered field by field with its basis (ML-01–ML-34); the Reasoner case as the archive's losing side, both runs held whole (ML-10, ML-08, ML-17), with #1725's account of it from Saville 1976 (D1725-01, D1725-02); the reading of the case, the critique that 'kept an organ and found a wider field' (O1725-01), within the mechanism of a base and form of the critics' own (O1725-02, O1725-03) and the conclusion's organ, holder and route (O1725-04, O1725-05), which the record applies to the archive and its Trust (ML-23, ML-24, the archive's reading); what the archive does not answer, the party leadership's own account of 1956 above all (ML-20, ML-21, ML-22), with the reuse terms the record calls 'not stated' standing beside the About page's CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (ML-26, ML-16 against F46); and the Capture Registry's account of the composition at the name (CAP-1-01–CAP-1-13). Not surfaced: every archive source; no card cites the census record or #1725.
